items.title: Tech EPS revisions +26.7% net — only two quarters since 2009 were higher
items.idea: A net 26.7% of S&P 1500 Tech names saw positive EPS revisions into Q3 season. Since 2009 only six other quarters hit a 20%+ spread and just two (Q3 09, Q1 10) were higher. Meanwhile S&P Q3 EPS growth is expected >25% for a third straight quarter, yet market-wide revisions skew slightly negative — so the upgrade cycle is a tech-only story.
items.angle: Revision breadth this extreme is crowding evidence and fundamental evidence at once. The two prior higher readings were post-crisis recoveries, not late-cycle AI capex.
items.tweetA: Tech revisions are at a level seen in only two quarters since 2009, both recoveries from a crash. This time the index is at highs and 89% of stocks aren't. Concentration of earnings upgrades is the same trade as concentration of price.
items.tweetB: Everyone else's EPS is being revised down while Tech's is being revised up 26.7% net. If the S&P prints 25% growth for a third quarter, ask how much of it is five companies. The beat is the easy part; the revision breadth is the crowded part.

items.title: Large caps overbought, small/micro oversold — SOXX vs RSP rotation
items.idea: Large-cap ETFs entered today overbought above 50-DMAs while small and micro caps sit oversold; mid caps neutral. September was awful for the average stock even as cap-weighted S&P held on mega-caps and semis. In the last week the average stock has started beating semis, and big consumer names bounced after a rough September on higher rates and oil.
items.angle: The index and the median stock are telling two different stories; the last week is the first sign of the median stock catching a bid at semis' expense.
items.tweetA: Large caps overbought, small caps oversold, mids neutral. That is not a rotation, it's a staircase. Someone is going to have to close the gap, and it is rarely the oversold side that gives up.
items.tweetB: Semis sold, equal-weight bid, same week. If you've been waiting for breadth to confirm the index, it may be arriving by the index's leaders coming down rather than the laggards going up.

items.title: 'Big software' charts are the best outside Energy after a 'dead industry' H1
items.idea: In H1 2026 software was treated as dead on AI obsolescence fears. Bespoke now says CRM, NOW and TEAM chart as well as anything outside Energy. Their point: some software loses to AI, others adapt and benefit — narratives flip faster than fundamentals.
items.angle: The 'AI eats SaaS' trade was the cleanest consensus short of H1; its unwind coincides with semis weakness. Watch for it being the funding leg of the rotation.
items.tweetA: In H1 software was a corpse. Now CRM, NOW and TEAM have the best charts in the market outside energy. The AI-eats-SaaS trade didn't get disproven, it got crowded.
items.tweetB: Semis down, software up, same week. Either the market just decided AI is a margin story for incumbents rather than a capex story for chipmakers, or it's a rotation that ends when the next hyperscaler guide lands.

items.source: Bespoke Investment Group / Morning Market Note
items.title: 10-yr yield below 5.19%, WTI above $92, Japan PPI -0.3% vs +0.5% expected
items.idea: The 10-year is down 5+ bps but still under 5.19%, WTI is lower >1% yet above $92, Nikkei fell ~2% for a fourth straight decline as Japan Sept PPI unexpectedly fell 0.3% (forecast +0.5%). German Sept CPI +0.6% m/m, in line, vs +0.2% in August. STOXX 600 +0.4% for a third day, helped by little tech exposure.
items.angle: A 10-year near 5.2% and oil at $92 is the macro backdrop under every equity multiple conversation. Japan's PPI miss against hot German CPI is a divergence worth keeping on the screen.
items.tweetA: 10-year near 5.2%, WTI at $92, and the debate is about AI sentiment. Whatever multiple you're paying for tech, it's being discounted at a rate that didn't exist in the last cycle.
items.tweetB: Japan PPI -0.3% when +0.5% was expected. Germany CPI +0.6% m/m versus 0.2% a month ago. Two big importers of the same oil, opposite price prints. One of those data points is wrong about the second-round effects.

items.source: Bespoke Investment Group / Morning Market Note
items.title: Waller: higher rates reflect growth, not inflation expectations; NFIB expansion plans at 4-month low
items.idea: Fed Governor Waller said the rise in rates is a function of stronger growth, not rising inflation expectations. Same morning NFIB Small Business Optimism came in weaker as uncertainty and inflation concerns rose and the 'good time to expand' share fell to a four-month low. Big-bank Q3 results were mixed vs expectations.
items.angle: A Fed voice framing the back-up in yields as benign growth, while small business says the opposite, is the cleanest bull/bear split in the data right now.
items.tweetA: Waller says yields are up because growth is strong. NFIB small businesses say expansion plans are at a four-month low. One of them is describing a different economy than the other.
items.tweetB: If higher rates are 'growth', the Fed can ignore them. If they are inflation risk premium, it can't. NFIB just gave the second explanation a data point.

items.source: Bespoke Investment Group / Morning Market Note
items.title: KOSPI -5%+ as Hock Tan: 'a lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in'
items.idea: KOSPI plunged more than 5% on AI concerns; Bespoke ties the worry to Broadcom CEO Hock Tan's comment that 'a lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in', raising fears sentiment has run ahead of fundamentals. Europe, with little tech exposure, held up while Asia sold.
items.angle: When the CEO of a primary AI beneficiary says the investor base doesn't understand the product, that is a sentiment signal. Korea is the high-beta expression because of memory.
items.tweetA: The head of Broadcom told the market it doesn't know what it owns. Korea, which owns the memory leg of that trade, dropped 5% the next day. $AVGO $MU
items.tweetB: Europe, with no tech to speak of, is up three days in a row. The AI-free index is the new defensive trade.

items.title: 'Almost Like Having a Printing Press' — be a buyer when commodity consensus is very bearish
items.idea: The issue's stated contention is that consistently profitable commodity trades come from buying when consensus is very bearish, and that this also bears on natural-resource equities. The body is a teaser; the full argument sits behind the paywall.
items.angle: Contrarian commodity framing arrives while oil is >$92 and lithium futures are plunging — one of those is a bearish consensus worth checking.
items.tweetA: Contrarian Investing 101 says buy when consensus is bearish. The harder part is finding a commodity with a bearish consensus and a catalyst. Lithium futures just broke on an EU rule. $ALB $SQM
items.tweetB: Oil at $92 is not a bearish-consensus market. The contrarian screen for commodities right now points elsewhere: battery metals, not barrels.

items.source: The Pragmatic Engineer / Gergely Orosz (Sam Newman excerpt)
items.title: Memory prices spiked in 2025–26 — clients can't secure ordinary cloud capacity
items.idea: Newman writes that GPU costs keep rising and memory costs spiked significantly in 2025 and 2026, hitting general server availability. Clients are struggling to run non-AI workloads on large public clouds because capacity can't be secured; shifting regions helps, buying hardware has lengthening lead times. DR plans that assume on-demand provisioning in a regional failure may find everyone fighting over scraps.
items.angle: The AI buildout is crowding out ordinary compute. Capacity reservation becomes a priced product — good for hyperscaler pricing power and memory suppliers.
items.tweetA: AI isn't just consuming the GPUs. Memory costs have spiked enough that engineers can't get plain vanilla cloud capacity. That is the second-order effect nobody has in a model. $MU $AMZN
items.tweetB: Disaster recovery plans assume you can spin up infrastructure when a region fails. If everyone does it at once, in a capacity-constrained world, you are bidding against the rest of the internet. Reserved capacity is the new insurance premium.

items.source: The Pragmatic Engineer / Gergely Orosz (Sam Newman excerpt)
items.title: Uber burned its annual AI budget in four months; Microsoft pulling Claude licenses on cost
items.idea: Cited examples: Uber reportedly spent its whole annual AI budget in the first four months; Microsoft is pulling Claude licenses from employees, partly on cost; an unsubstantiated Axios report says an unnamed enterprise spent $500M on Claude licenses without cost controls. Nordhealth's CTO cites a QA engineer spending €1,000 in one week on Claude Code and more than doubling productivity.
items.angle: AI budgets are variable cost and blow through plan. A €1,000/week seat is cheaper than a day of a fully loaded engineer — but a $500M accident isn't.
items.tweetA: Uber used a year of AI budget in four months. Microsoft is pulling licences over cost. A QA engineer burned €1,000 in a week and doubled output. Both are true, which is why nobody can forecast token demand. $UBER $MSFT
items.tweetB: €1,000 a week for an engineer who doubled output is a bargain. The same invoice with no controls is $500M. Procurement for AI looks nothing like procurement for software seats.

items.source: The Pragmatic Engineer / Gergely Orosz (Sam Newman excerpt)
items.title: Cursor pays Anthropic and competes with Claude Code — vendor-on-vendor dependency risk
items.idea: Newman: Cursor had to pass on a significant cost increase in 2025 after Anthropic changed pricing, while Anthropic's Claude Code competes directly with Cursor. His advice: be multi-model, multi-vendor, review AI vendors more often, and check whether a vendor depends wholly on a single provider. Mixed-vendor flows also compound availability risk because all models must be up.
items.angle: Wrapper companies are structurally exposed to the model owners' pricing and roadmap. It is the same supplier-competitor structure the market worried about in cloud.
items.tweetA: Cursor buys its best input from a company that sells a direct competitor. The wrapper layer is a supplier-competitor relationship with a price that can be changed unilaterally.
items.tweetB: A three-vendor AI flow has the availability of all three multiplied together. Multi-model strategies reduce pricing risk and raise outage risk at the same time.

items.source: The Pragmatic Engineer / Gergely Orosz (Sam Newman excerpt)
items.title: Coinbase outage: ~$7B of activity interrupted by a single AWS zone, no automated failover
items.idea: Gergely recounts Coinbase's global trading service going offline after one AWS zone failed. His napkin math: Coinbase moves ~$5.2T per year, was valued ~$40B, and the outage interrupted ~$7B of financial activity; he calls no automated failover 'incredibly amateurish' for that scale. Also: AI agents writing more code means more deploys and more incidents.
items.angle: Resilience is an under-priced operational risk in crypto infrastructure and in AI-generated code volume.
items.tweetA: $5.2T a year of volume, no automated failover, one AWS zone down. The tail risk in crypto isn't a hack, it's an availability zone. $COIN
items.tweetB: More AI-written code means more deploys means more incidents. The productivity gain from agents shows up in the output and the outage log at the same time.

items.title: AI personas barely move forecasts: 60.6% vs 84% market-implied probability
items.idea: UChicago researchers ran 1,296 possible AI personas (age, risk tolerance, etc.), testing 54 per event on prediction-market contracts. Personas mostly agreed with each other; the AI gave the eventual outcome 60.6% on average versus 84% implied by market prices — a 23-point gap, near coin-flip. Persona instructions are 'a continuation of the prompt rather than a stored belief'. A fake market price test and analyst comparison sit behind the paywall.
items.angle: Prompting an LLM to 'think like Buffett' doesn't change what it believes. It's a calibration problem: the model is systematically underconfident vs markets.
items.tweetA: Tell an LLM it's Warren Buffett and its forecast moves barely at all. On prediction markets it put 60.6% on what happened; traders were at 84%. The model isn't underconfident because it's cautious, it just doesn't know. $NVDA
items.tweetB: 1,296 personas, all agreeing with each other. The diversity of opinions is a prompt artifact. That's why an 'AI hedge fund' of ten personas is one forecaster with ten hats.

charts.desc: Persona prompt template shown as image in article. Charts inside — worth opening

items.title: 89% of names are >10% below early-June highs while the index sits at all-time highs
items.idea: Citing Martin Pelletier, the author says 89% of names are down more than 10% from early-June highs while the market is basically at all-time highs — 'a really unique year where the market is at highs but most names are struggling'. SPY continues to flag over the 8 EMA in a bullish consolidation.
items.angle: This is the breadth divergence in one number. Combined with Bespoke's rotation, it frames why the average portfolio feels bad in an up market.
items.tweetA: 89% of stocks are more than 10% below June highs and the index is at a record. 'Market's fine' and 'my portfolio hurts' are both accurate.
items.tweetB: A narrow market is a one-trade market. The index is a bet on a handful of names while the rest of the market is already in a drawdown.

items.title: Korean margin calls 'every single night' — KOSPI -5.5% overnight, AI names flushed then bid back
items.idea: Overnight KOSPI fell 5.5%, which the author says weighed on his tech names. He claims Korea has seen margin calls seemingly every night recently. The AI names flushed overnight but many were bid to green by the US session.
items.angle: Leveraged retail unwinding in Korea is a global memory/AI risk transmitter. US dip-buying reflex remains intact.
items.tweetA: KOSPI fell 5.5% and the margin-call stories are nightly now. US AI names were green by lunch. The dip-buying reflex is intact, but the leverage is somewhere else.
items.tweetB: Korea is where AI leverage is visible: retail margin, memory supply chain, a 5% daily move. US doesn't see it until it's in the tape. $005930

items.title: 'Artificial' (Guadagnino's OpenAI film, out Dec 25, 2026) reviewed as a sprawling mess
items.idea: Review of Luca Guadagnino's film about the OpenAI board firing Sam Altman, told through Ilya Sutskever (Andrew Garfield as Altman). The reviewer: unfocused, tours Sutskever's career from 2003, ChatGPT launches off-screen, 'the true story of OpenAI is stranger and scarier'. Releases Dec 25, 2026.
items.angle: AI industry is now mainstream cultural material. A Christmas Day tentpole about OpenAI's governance fight is a cultural marker of peak AI narrative.
items.tweetA: They made a film about the OpenAI board coup and released it on Christmas Day. When your boardroom drama is a mainstream movie, you are in the cultural phase of the cycle. $MSFT
items.tweetB: The Social Network came out in 2010, when Facebook was six years old. A movie about OpenAI at age ten — when it's a $100B+ question — is less a verdict than a bookmark.

items.source: This Week in Startups / TWiST Ticker
items.title: Character.AI files Chapter 11; Disney gets assets and perpetual tech licence for $20M
items.idea: Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 and agreed to sell assets plus a perpetual technology licence to Disney for $20M — described as one of the first major bankruptcies of the generative AI boom.
items.angle: A consumer AI companion platform with huge usage and a $20M exit is the first dent in the 'usage = value' narrative. Contrast with $200M rounds for robot builders the same day.
items.tweetA: Character.AI: Chapter 11, assets sold to Disney for $20M. The perpetual licence went for $20M. Usage isn't revenue and revenue isn't margin.
items.tweetB: The first big gen-AI bankruptcy isn't a foundation model, it's a chatbot app. The ones that go first are the ones paying inference on every message with no moat.

items.source: This Week in Startups / TWiST Ticker
items.title: Microsoft unveils Maia 300; Meta launches Muse Wonder / Wonder Full agent models
items.idea: Microsoft's Maia 300 is billed as reducing reliance on Nvidia. Meta launched Muse Wonder and Wonder Full — agent-focused models built to persist through complex coding and professional tasks and keep context. Workday also agreed to buy C1.ai for access control of employees and AI agents.
items.angle: Custom silicon from all hyperscalers is the long-term bear case for merchant GPUs. Agent-persistence is the capability shift worth watching.
items.tweetA: Third-generation Maia. Google has TPUs, Amazon has Trainium, now Microsoft has Maia 300. Every one of Nvidia's biggest customers builds a substitute. $NVDA $MSFT
items.tweetB: Meta says its new model is built to persist through complex tasks and keep context. The metric that matters in 2027 is how long an agent can work without a human.

items.source: This Week in Startups / TWiST Ticker
items.title: Bending Spoons cuts a large share of Airtable's staff one month after $1.28B purchase
items.idea: Bending Spoons laid off a large, undisclosed share of Airtable's workforce one month after buying it for $1.28B. The company faces backlash over the bluntness of its announcement.
items.angle: Bending Spoons is the playbook for the SaaS endgame: buy at depressed multiple, cut to profitability. If software valuations stay low, expect more.
items.tweetA: Bought for $1.28B. Layoffs a month later. The new owner of mid-cap software isn't a strategic, it's a cost-cut machine. That is the floor under SaaS valuations.
items.tweetB: Public-to-private software with immediate headcount cuts is the real AI-disruption transmission. Not AI replacing the product, but the owner replacing the staff.

items.source: This Week in Startups / TWiST Ticker
items.title: Funding: ICON $200M Series D (robotic construction), Ubitium $14M seed, Causa Prima $20M, HyLight €13M
items.idea: ICON raised $200M co-led by Baillie Gifford and BlackRock, plus an Austin R&D center. Ubitium raised $14M for a universal processor for robots/drones/machines. Causa Prima (AI finance) $20M seed led by Base10. HyLight (hydrogen airships for inspection) €13M. Undecimal Bio (RNA delivery) €16M seed.
items.angle: Physical AI (construction, robotics, processors) is attracting growth equity from BlackRock-type names at a time when software AI is questioned.
items.tweetA: BlackRock and Baillie Gifford wrote a $200M cheque into robotic construction. The institutional money is moving from chatbots to things that pour concrete. $BLK
items.tweetB: A universal processor for robots at $14M seed. Everything with a motor needs a brain. The question is whether the brain is a general chip or a specialised one.

items.source: This Week in Startups / TWiST Ticker
items.title: Podcast: mesh networks on Ukraine's front lines; Flock licence-plate-reader backlash
items.idea: The linked TWiST episode covers Totem, an offline compass for finding friends at festivals using a mesh network (more devices strengthen the mesh), mesh networks on the front lines in Ukraine, why phones fail in big crowds, hardware fundraising in an AI world, and the backlash against Flock licence-plate readers.
items.angle: Mesh networking is a growing theme as connectivity infrastructure becomes a target.
items.tweetA: More devices make a mesh stronger, not weaker. In an era where data centers and cables are on Iran's target list, that's a different networking design principle.
items.tweetB: Flock licence plate readers are facing backlash while mesh networks are protecting soldiers in Ukraine. Same tech, opposite sides of a privacy argument.

items.source: McKinsey / Banking Practice (Ishaan Seth, Stephanie Hauser)
items.title: UK banks at strong returns, but neobanks/fintechs hold ~27% of UK banking relationships
items.idea: UK banks are enjoying some of their strongest returns in years, but competitive advantage is shifting: neobanks and fintechs hold about 27% of UK banking relationships as customers spread activity across providers. Three races: customers and deposits, the commercial transaction layer (payments, liquidity), and AI-driven cost-base rebuild. Email is a teaser.
items.angle: Relationship fragmentation means deposit stickiness is lower — a margin risk for the high-NIM era.
items.tweetA: UK bank returns are the best in years, and 27% of relationships already sit with neobanks. Peak earnings and structural share loss in the same year. $LLOY $NWG
items.tweetB: The prize isn't lending, it's the transaction layer. Whoever owns payments and liquidity owns the data that prices credit.

items.title: Siemens's next reinvention: interview with Cedrik Neike — 'Navigate the next era of manufacturing'
items.idea: The email only carries a teaser: as technology transforms the factory floor, industrials are asking what it takes to lead the next era of manufacturing. Companion links: 'How AI-led commercial transformation can power industrial growth' and 'The symbiotic enterprise'. Full interview not in email.
items.angle: Siemens is a read-through for industrial software, automation and grid demand. Charts and detail inside the article.
items.tweetA: Siemens' Cedrik Neike is being asked what leads the next era of manufacturing. The answer is likely software — the hardware is the delivery mechanism. $SIE
items.tweetB: Industrial automation is the physical-AI beneficiary with less hype than the chip names. Worth reading what Siemens says about order books.

items.title: SR007 Demo Day: 80 companies, 2,000+ investor RSVPs, deep-tech tilt
items.idea: 80 SR007 companies pitched at the Palace of Fine Arts; 2,000+ investors RSVP'd, 954 seats full with overflow. The cohort leaned robotics, space, manufacturing and defense; Kanu (SR005) raised an $11.7M seed to bring AGI to enterprise. Applications for SR008 close Nov 1 ($1M + $10M credits).
items.angle: The accelerator pipeline is tilting to atoms: robotics, space, defense. $1M plus $10M credits shows compute credits are now currency.
items.tweetA: 2,000 investors RSVP'd to watch 80 companies pitch, and the crowds were around the hardware, robotics and space booths. Capital is migrating from apps to atoms.
items.tweetB: $1M cash plus $10M in compute credits. The credits are worth ten times the cash. The cost of starting a company has become mostly a GPU bill.

items.title: Robots inside data centres and orbital lasers for missile defence: SR007 deep-tech picks
items.idea: Cybernetic Physics deploys autonomous robots in data centres for rack-and-stack, cabling, maintenance 24/7. PhotonSpear is building orbital lasers for missile defence. Oruk builds speech models that capture tone and emotion. ChronoSpace builds world models for manufacturing/retail/construction. Colmez: agentic platform for hazardous-waste.
items.angle: Data-centre labour is a bottleneck for the buildout; robotics there is a direct read-through for capex timelines. Defence tech remains a venture magnet.
items.tweetA: Autonomous robots for rack-and-stack in data centres. The AI buildout is constrained by electricians and technicians. The picks-and-shovels of the picks-and-shovels.
items.tweetB: A startup is pitching orbital lasers for missile defence. It's a Demo Day, not a defence budget — but the fact that it draws the crowd tells you where capital thinks 2030 is heading.

items.title: CMS won't renew 2.5% Medicare boost; real Medicare physician pay -33% since 2001
items.idea: CMS has no plans to renew a temporary 2.5% Medicare reimbursement boost expiring end-2026; commercial plans benchmark to Medicare so it cascades. 84% of medical groups report higher operating costs, up 11% on average. Inflation-adjusted Medicare physician pay is down 33% since 2001.
items.angle: Specialty practice margin squeeze is a roll-up and private-equity risk and a driver of AI adoption.
items.tweetA: Medicare physician pay is down 33% in real terms since 2001. A 2.5% boost expires in December. Practices are not going to cut costs more; they'll look for any revenue lever. That's the AI sales pitch.
items.tweetB: Commercial insurers price off Medicare schedules. A federal cut isn't a federal problem — it reprices every contract in the country. $UNH $HCA

items.title: AI phone agents: 18% daytime missed calls, 81% after hours; Piedmont +17% appointments
items.idea: Prosper AI's CallIQ study of ~2,000 practices in 29 states found an 18% daytime missed-call rate and 81% after-hours; 19% of provider schedules go unfilled. Piedmont Plastic Surgery & Dermatology (37 providers) saw appointments rise from 19,209 to 22,524 (+17%) in Aug 2026; at $392/visit, 3,315 extra appointments is ~$1.3M in a month. Claimed total opportunity: ~$125K per physician ($108B overall). Study is vendor-produced.
items.angle: Voice AI replaces missed calls; the economics are clear at practice level. Treat the market-size figure with vendor-bias discount.
items.tweetA: 81% of calls to specialty practices are missed after hours. One dermatology group put an AI on the phones and booked 3,315 more appointments in a month — about $1.3M. That is the clearest AI ROI I have seen that doesn't involve cutting staff.
items.tweetB: $108B is a vendor-sized TAM with a vendor-run study. But the 22,524 vs 19,209 appointments figure is something an analyst can check. Is voice AI the first agent product with a boring, measurable ROI?

items.title: What Meta's Muse gets right: a specialised agent, briefly the #1 app
items.idea: Meta's Muse is an agentic personal assistant that runs your digital life (schedule, food orders, phone calls) and was briefly the most downloaded app in early October 2026. The author argues it beat frontier labs by specialising rather than building general models, with roots in the OpenClaw craze (OpenAI acquired OpenClaw). The cost: handing over credit cards, inboxes and medical details to Meta.
items.angle: Consumer distribution beats model quality; Meta's problem is trust, not tech. A top-of-store position shows consumer demand for agents.
items.tweetA: Meta's laggard model topped the app store because it did something specific: run your life. The frontier labs sell generalists; consumers apparently want an employee. $META
items.tweetB: The product that needs your credit card, medical info and inbox is being built by the company with the worst privacy record. The adoption curve will tell us what consumers will trade for convenience.

items.title: RBA hiked 100bp to 4.6%; inflation 3.8% → 4.6% (March) → 4.0%; unemployment 4.1% → 4.6%
items.idea: Australia tightened first this year when labour and inflation heated: unemployment fell 4.3%→4.1% then rose to 4.6%. Inflation surged from ~3.8% to 4.6% by March and is back to 4.0%. The RBA hiked 100bp to 4.6%. Author thinks a bit more is possible but the economy is responding. AUDUSD was the original expression.
items.angle: A template for how a tightening cycle works in 2026: 100bp and inflation down 60bp, but unemployment up 50bp. Which central bank is next?
items.tweetA: Australia: 100bp of hikes, inflation from 4.6% down to 4.0%, unemployment up from 4.1% to 4.6%. That is the price of getting 60bp. Other central banks are about to find out what it costs.
items.tweetB: The RBA is the canary. If a 100bp cycle needed 50bp of unemployment, how does the Fed do it from a 10-year at 5.2%? $AUDUSD

items.title: Ledger supply-chain theft hits $103M; Coinbase BTC premium lowest since July; ETFs shed $680M in a week
items.idea: BTC $83,231 (+1%), BTC dominance 59.8%, ETH $2,501, SOL $106 (-4%), 24h liquidations $813M, Fear & Greed 56. Ledger's supply-chain attack (CryptoBilis) losses reach $103M. Coinbase BTC premium is lowest since July; BTC ETFs -$65M and ETH ETFs -$85M on the day, -$680M in a week; K33 says US BTC transfers likely custody-related.
items.angle: Custody security and ETF flow weakness while alts lead lower is a risk-off crypto tape.
items.tweetA: BTC ETFs lost $680M this week, the Coinbase premium is at a July low and Ledger lost $103M to a supply-chain attack. Demand is fading and the risk is in the self-custody wrappers. $BTC $COIN
items.tweetB: A hardware wallet supply-chain attack is a worse headline for crypto than an exchange hack. The product's whole value proposition is not trusting the middleman.

items.title: Russia opens crypto: Sberbank authorised to exchange, MOEX BTC for retail Dec 1, sanctioned A7 launches USDT service
items.idea: Russia authorises Sberbank to exchange crypto; Moscow Exchange to open BTC to retail on Dec 1; sanctioned Russian payment network A7 unveils a USDT service. Separately South Korea blocks KuCoin, MEXC, BingX and 24 more exchanges.
items.angle: A sanctioned state is building domestic crypto rails and stablecoin settlement. USDT is the sanction-evasion rail again.
items.tweetA: Sberbank can exchange crypto, MOEX opens BTC to retail December 1, and a sanctioned payments network launches USDT service. Russia's sanctions workaround is now a regulated market. $USDT
items.tweetB: South Korea blocked 27 exchanges while Russia opened its largest exchange to retail BTC. The regulatory map of crypto is being drawn by geopolitics.

items.title: FSB: $300B stablecoin market not crisis-ready; Morgan Stanley delays tokenised stocks to Q1 2027
items.idea: The FSB says the $300B stablecoin market is not crisis-ready. Morgan Stanley delays tokenised stocks to Q1 2027, while Robinhood's tokenised stocks go live on Hedera and Bybit launches US stock trading (1,000+ stocks/ETFs). CME adds UNI futures. Australia moves to regulate crypto-settled CFDs. Binance exec says TradFi hedge funds are exploring crypto arbitrage.
items.angle: Tokenisation is shipping at crypto-native firms while incumbents delay. The FSB warning is the regulatory overhang.
items.tweetA: The FSB says the $300B stablecoin market isn't crisis-ready. Morgan Stanley delayed tokenised stocks to 2027 and Robinhood shipped them today. The retail brokers are beating the banks on settlement. $HOOD $MS
items.tweetB: Stablecoins are $300B and the supervisor's own statement is that nobody knows how a run would work. That's the sentence that comes before a rule.

items.title: Solana halves slot time to 200ms; Aptos encrypted mempool; Monad compliance tools; Strategy, BitMine buying
items.idea: Solana halves target slot time to 200ms; Aptos launches an encrypted mempool; Monad adds confidentiality/compliance tools; Strategy buys 250 BTC and $192M STRC; BitMine buys 12.5K ETH; Justin Sun holds $2.25B onchain; Binance Pool to shut Nov 10; Blur frontend closing Nov 12; ZEC and HYPE lead the slump.
items.angle: Technical roadmaps point to institutional-grade features (privacy, compliance, speed) while treasury buyers keep accumulating.
items.tweetA: Solana at 200ms slots, Aptos with encrypted mempools, Monad adding compliance tooling. The chains are building for an institutional counterparty who hasn't arrived yet. $SOL
items.tweetB: Strategy bought 250 BTC while ETFs are bleeding. The treasury-company bid is now the marginal buyer, which is a different kind of fragility.

items.title: Dollar at 18-month high; BlackRock cuts US stocks to neutral, GS turns bullish; gold $4,190, Nasdaq 27,250
items.idea: Dollar hits an 18-month high. BlackRock cuts US stocks to neutral and favours bonds; Goldman turns bullish on stocks for the rest of 2026. Nasdaq $27,250, gold $4,190. Week ahead: CPI, PPI, Warsh speaks, earnings begin.
items.angle: Two big houses moving in opposite directions on the same day tells you nothing about the market and something about positioning.
items.tweetA: BlackRock goes neutral on US equities, Goldman turns bullish. Same day. When the two biggest research desks disagree this loudly, the index is trading on flows, not forecasts. $SPY
items.tweetB: Dollar at an 18-month high with gold at $4,190. Both bid at once says it's not a pure dollar story; it's a flight from something else.

items.title: Private credit defaults hit record 6.3%; Fitch warns France faces potential downgrade
items.idea: Private credit defaults hit a record 6.3% (via X post). Fitch warns France faces a potential downgrade. China lithium futures plunge on the EU hybrid cap.
items.angle: Record private credit defaults while public indices make highs; sovereign stress in Europe's second-largest economy.
items.tweetA: Private credit defaults at a record 6.3% and the S&P is at highs. The asset class that replaced bank lending is the first to show losses, and it's not marked to market. $BX $APO
items.tweetB: Fitch on France: potential downgrade. With the 10-year near 5.2%, the sovereign credit story in Europe is a fiscal arithmetic problem.

items.title: 10+ supertankers reverse off Fujairah; UK blames Iran for plot on US bomber base; Iran threatens cables and data centres
items.idea: More than 10 supertankers approaching Fujairah reversed course amid Iranian attacks. The UK blames Iran for a plot against a US bomber base; Iran accuses the UK of a false flag. Iran threatens to attack cables and data centres. Oil falls on possible higher supply from Russia (WTI still >$92 per Bespoke).
items.angle: Energy chokepoint plus digital infrastructure threats: the AI buildout now has a physical-security risk premium.
items.tweetA: Ten-plus supertankers turned around off Fujairah, and Iran is threatening data centres and undersea cables in the same news cycle. Oil is falling on Russian supply hopes. That's a pricing mismatch. $XOM
items.tweetB: Iran's target list now includes cables and data centres. The AI trade assumes physical infrastructure is safe. It's the one assumption nobody models.

items.title: US weighs cutting Starlink in Ukraine; Putin offers pause only on election day; Ukraine strikes cripple Yandex
items.idea: US weighs cutting Starlink access in Ukraine; Trump says Putin wants a deal more than Zelenskyy; Putin offers to pause attacks only on election day; Ukraine strikes cripple Yandex connectivity (data centres targeted).
items.angle: Starlink is a single point of failure for Ukrainian comms; data centres are legitimate targets in the war.
items.tweetA: Ukraine's battlefield network runs on one American company's terminal, and Washington is weighing turning it off. Infrastructure dependence is geopolitical leverage. $SPACEX
items.tweetB: Yandex's connectivity collapsed after strikes on data centres. A cloud region is a military target now.

items.title: Cyber: French supermarket fridges hacked to 122°F; Japan declares 'state of emergency in cyberspace'
items.idea: Hackers heated French supermarket fridges to 122°F, causing fires; Japan declares a 'state of emergency in cyberspace'. Context: Iran threatening cables and data centres; Yandex hit.
items.angle: Cyber to physical-damage attacks are escalating. Insurance and industrial control systems exposure.
items.tweetA: Hackers heated supermarket fridges in France to 122°F. Japan declared a cyber emergency. Cyber risk has crossed from data loss to cold-chain loss. $CRWD
items.tweetB: A fridge hack is a food-supply attack. The next step is a grid or water system.

items.title: China lithium futures plunge on EU hybrid cap; oil falls on potential Russian supply
items.idea: Chinese lithium futures plunge after the EU hybrid cap deals a fresh blow to battery demand. Oil falls on potential higher supply from Russia. BlackRock favouring bonds.
items.angle: EU policy on hybrids hits lithium demand — policy-driven commodity demand shock.
items.tweetA: The EU capped hybrids and Chinese lithium futures dropped. A regulation written in Brussels reprices a futures curve in Guangzhou. $ALB
items.tweetB: Oil lower on Russian supply hopes, lithium lower on EU demand rules. Both bearish commodity stories arrive as Haymaker says buy bearish consensus.

items.title: AI slump on CXMT chip and Hock Tan comments; KOSPI halted; Nvidia halts RTX 5090 for AI chips; AMD sees CPU TAM >$200B by 2030
items.idea: AI slumps on a CXMT chip (China memory) and Hock Tan's comments; KOSPI halted as AI panic spreads. Nvidia reportedly halts RTX 5090 production to prioritise AI chips; AMD says CPU demand could top $200B by 2030; US rejects power cuts to data centres in grid emergencies; IonQ to buy Elisity for up to $1.3B.
items.angle: A Chinese memory chip hitting AI sentiment connects Korea's selloff to China's catch-up. Gamers lose GPUs to AI.
items.tweetA: China's CXMT shows a chip and Korea gets halted. The memory trade priced Samsung and Hynix as a duopoly with growth. $005930 $MU
items.tweetB: Nvidia stopped making the 5090 to make AI chips. Gamers are the swing supplier of the AI buildout. And the US just ruled data centres can't be cut in a grid emergency — power priority is now policy.

items.title: Anthropic cuts distiller-harvested data 90–99%; Epic orders devs to use Claude; SpaceXSI merges Grok/Cursor/X; OpenAI to revive Sora
items.idea: Anthropic reportedly cuts data harvested by distillers by 90-99%. Epic Games reportedly orders developers to use Claude. 'SpaceXSI' merges Grok, Cursor and X Premium. OpenAI plans to revive Sora. Meta bans ByteDance ads. AI testing officials move to the White House.
items.angle: Distillation defence is an IP moat; enterprise mandates (Epic) are demand signals.
items.tweetA: Anthropic says it cut distillation extraction by 90–99%. If true, the open-weights catch-up relied on stolen outputs has a speed limit. $AMZN $GOOGL
items.tweetB: A games company ordering developers to use one model is the clearest enterprise-adoption signal: mandates, not experiments.

items.title: Netflix readies layoffs of ~5% of staff, shares down 42% this year
items.idea: Netflix reportedly readies its first major layoffs since 2022, cutting 5% of staff, with shares down 42% this year (per ZeroHedge). Same issue: Airtable cuts, and IonQ buys Elisity.
items.angle: Layoffs at a streaming leader mean content-cost and AI-efficiency repricing.
items.tweetA: Netflix is down 42% this year and planning to cut 5% of staff. The streaming winner of the last decade is now the one cutting.
items.tweetB: Layoffs at Netflix and Airtable the same week. Efficiency is the story for every mature tech name.
